Visa reforms an 'attack' on public service workers, says UNISON
Under plans set out by the home secretary, the qualification period for many key workers to settle in the UK would treble, UNISON tells TUC
Date posted: 15 September 2026

In a speech to delegates in Brighton, UNISON senior vice president Debbie Rowden urged the government to rethink proposals that will drive away international staff despite workforce shortages in critical public service roles.

Moving a composite motion calling for the withdrawal of the visa changes, Debbie said: "Instead of the five years to settlement that was originally promised, the government now wants to keep them waiting for 15 years.
"They specifically targeted UNISON members working in health and social care, saying their work was 'low waged and low skilled'.
"The government wants to give bankers a three-year route to settlement. But social care workers will be kept waiting for 15 years. The same for nursing auxiliaries, theatre nurses, health care assistants, children's residential care workers, probation service workers and more."

UNISON has been campaigning for months against the changes through its Fair Visa Campaign, lobbying MPs and taking the issue to Downing Street.

The union wants the increase in the qualification period for settlement (also known as indefinite leave to remain) to be dropped. Another key part of the campaign is to change visa sponsorship rules so migrant care workers are no longer tied to a single employer, which should reduce exploitation.

--- BBC VERSION, same TUC debate, approved source ---
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8d0nj04g6o  (Exa metadata: 2026-09-15T10:25:28Z)
"Under the government's proposals the standard wait to qualify for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain, would increase to 10 years.
People who arrived on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait, while those who relied on benefits for more than 12 months would have to wait 20 years.
The changes would not apply to people who have already obtained settlement but would cover people already living in the UK, including those who had been expecting to get permanence residence in the coming months."
Unison senior vice president Debbie Rowden: "The government wants to give bankers a three-year route to settlement, but social care workers will be kept waiting for 15 years."
"The motion, which also called for the five-year route to settlement to be retained for workers, was passed unanimously by delegates."
